---
title: "Code execution & the kernel"
---

Our `post.qmd` has a single `{python}` cell. This chapter is what happens when it
runs, and, more to the point, the lengths qmd-fast goes to so that it usually
*doesn't have to*.

Executing `{python}` / `{r}` cells is the most involved subsystem and lives
entirely in the **server** (`crates/server`), in two layers: the **executor**
(`exec.rs`) decides *what* to run and splices outputs back into the block list;
the **kernel** (`kernel.rs`) is one warm Jupyter process it talks to over ZMQ.
The core knows nothing about execution: it emits code cells as blocks, and the
server fills in their outputs.

## The executor (`exec.rs`)

`Executor` holds **one warm kernel per language**, created lazily, plus the two
output caches that let it skip work, one in memory and one on disk:

```rust
struct Executor {
    python: PathBuf,            // QMD_FAST_PYTHON (default python3)
    r: PathBuf,                 // QMD_FAST_R (default R)
    langs: HashMap<&'static str, LangState>,  // "python" / "r" → warm kernel + ran-list
    freeze: FreezeCache,        // persistent _freeze/ output cache (on disk)
    no_exec: bool,              // QMD_FAST_NO_EXEC / --no-exec: render cells as source
    force_next: bool,           // "Restart kernel" forces a full re-run next rebuild
}
```

`run(blocks)` is the entry point each rebuild calls. Its very first check is the
`no_exec` flag: with `QMD_FAST_NO_EXEC` (or `--no-exec`) set, it returns the blocks
untouched, so every code cell previews as highlighted source with no kernel started and
no "kernel unavailable" notice. That makes `--no-exec` the safe way to open a document
you don't trust, and a `--host` preview without it logs a warning (exposing an executing
preview runs code on every save). Otherwise it groups the cells by language (preserving
document order), runs each language's cells, and splices an **output block after each
cell**:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  blocks["block list (cells marked)"] --> group["group cells by language"]
  group --> co["compute_outputs per language"]
  co --> splice["splice an output block after each cell<br/>(id derived from the cell id)"]
  splice --> out["block list + outputs"]
```

An output block's id is derived from its cell's id, so when a cell re-runs only
*its* output block changes: the diff swaps it in place (see
[the block model](block-model.qmd)).

## What runs on a rebuild

`compute_outputs` gives the document notebook semantics without re-running
everything. Per language, it answers one question, which **contiguous range** of
cells must actually execute, by sorting the cells into three zones
(@fig-exec-zones):

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-exec-zones
%%| fig-cap: "Each language's cells split into three zones; only the run range boots the kernel."
flowchart LR
  A["warm prefix<br/>the live kernel<br/>already ran it"] --> B["run range<br/>changed cell +<br/>everything downstream"] --> C["cached tail<br/>restored from<br/>_freeze/"]
```

The boundaries come from one key per cell: a **cumulative content hash**
(`freeze::cumulative_hashes`) that folds in the interpreter identity plus *every
same-language cell's code up to and including this one*. Because it is cumulative,
editing a cell moves its key **and every downstream key**, so an upstream edit
invalidates everything after it automatically, exactly the dependency a notebook
needs. `plan` then finds the warm prefix the live kernel already holds and the run
range; any suffix whose keys are already on disk is restored without running.

So editing the last cell re-runs one cell; editing the first re-runs all. The
kernel stays warm across all of it: no per-edit cold start (goal #3). A
`#| include: false` cell still runs (for its kernel-state side effects) but emits
no output block; a `#| cache: false` cell always re-runs and is never cached.

### The cumulative-hash chain in detail

The whole scheme rests on one tiny function. For a language's cells in document
order, `cumulative_hashes(interp, codes)` folds each cell's code into the running
digest of everything before it:

```text
key₀ = FNV1a( seed )
keyᵢ = FNV1a( keyᵢ₋₁  +  "\n"  +  codeᵢ )      (each digest is the 16-hex string of the previous)
```

The chain is seeded not by an empty string but by the **interpreter identity**, a
stable id of the form

```text
python::/path/to/python3::Python 3.11.9
```

built by `interp_id`: the language, the resolved interpreter path, and the first
line of `<program> --version`, run once and memoised. Because the seed flows into
*every* key, swapping the interpreter (a Python upgrade, a different `QMD_FAST_PYTHON`)
shifts the whole chain at once, so the old interpreter's cached outputs are never
served by a new one. Worked through for two cells `x = 1` then `print(x)`:

```text
seed  = "python::…::Python 3.11.9"
key₀  = FNV1a( seed + "\n" + "x = 1" )
key₁  = FNV1a( key₀ + "\n" + "print(x)" )
```

Edit `x = 1` to `x = 2` and `key₀` moves; because `key₁` is computed *from* `key₀`,
it moves too, even though `print(x)` is byte-for-byte unchanged. That is the
upstream-invalidation property the planner relies on, and it falls straight out of
the chaining: there is no separate dependency graph to keep correct. (FNV-1a is the
same 64-bit hash the core uses for block ids, chosen because it is small,
deterministic, and stable across runs and tool versions, so a cache written today
still hits tomorrow.)

## The persistent cache (`_freeze/`)

The warm prefix only exists while a kernel is alive. To skip work *across* `build`
runs and preview restarts (when the kernel holds nothing), outputs are also
written to `_freeze/<page>.json`, keyed by the **same** cumulative hash
(`crates/server/src/freeze.rs`). On a **cold start** the in-memory prefix is empty,
so if every cell's key hits the disk cache the whole document **replays from disk
and never boots the kernel**: an unchanged doc builds instantly. The kernel starts
only when a key is missing (a real edit), and only for the changed range.

`post.qmd` makes this vivid. Build it twice without touching it and the second
build replays the plot from `_freeze/` without ever starting Python. Bump `tau` to
12 and only that one cell's key misses, so only it re-runs; had there been cells
*after* it, their keys would have moved too, and they would re-run as well.

That cumulative key is what makes this safe where Quarto's per-cell `cache` is
fragile. It encodes *every byte of code the kernel ran to reach this output*, so:

- **a stale hit is impossible by construction**: no mtime heuristics, nothing to
  clear by hand; the content *is* the key;
- a different interpreter (say a Python upgrade) busts every key, since it can't
  serve outputs the old one computed;
- kernel **variable state is deliberately never cached** (that is the fragile part
  of per-cell caching), which is why a cold start can only skip a cell when its
  *whole upstream* is unchanged, never an arbitrary one in the middle.

What's stored is just the cell's output HTML (kernel images are already inline data
URIs, so there are no sidecar files).

### The on-disk file

`_freeze/<stem>.json` mirrors the source tree (`posts/x.qmd` caches to
`_freeze/posts/x.json`) so it's easy to inspect, and holds a flat, versioned list of
key/output pairs:

```json
{
  "version": 2,
  "entries": [
    { "k": "9f1c…", "v": "<pre class=\"qmd-stream\">…</pre>" },
    { "k": "a37e…", "v": "<img class=\"qmd-fig qmd-fig-light\" …>" }
  ]
}
```

A few properties earn their place:

- **`version` gating.** The loader compares `version` against the binary's
  `FORMAT_VERSION` and, on a mismatch, treats the file as **empty** rather than
  replaying entries it might no longer be able to interpret. The version is bumped
  not only when the file shape changes but when the *bundled output format* of a
  cached cell changes (the cell code is identical, so the cumulative key wouldn't
  move on its own); the next save rewrites the file fresh. A missing or corrupt file
  is tolerated the same way: start empty, rewrite on the next save.
- **Oldest-first order.** `entries` is written oldest-first so eviction can drop from
  the front. The cache keeps up to `MAX_ENTRIES` (1024) per page in a small
  LRU-ish set: a `put` moves the touched key to the most-recent end, and once the set
  is over the cap the front (least-recently-touched) entries are evicted. Because the
  live set is usually a few dozen cells, this holds a deep edit history while staying
  small on disk, which is why toggling an edit back and forth keeps restoring
  instantly instead of re-running.
- **Atomic write.** A save serialises to a sibling `*.json.tmp` and renames it into
  place, so a crash mid-write can't corrupt an existing cache; `_freeze/` (and any
  sub-dirs) are created on demand, and a write failure is logged but non-fatal (the
  build still works, just uncached).

### What is never persisted

The planner is deliberately stingy about what it hands the cache, so a bad result
can never bake in:

- **Error outputs** (anything carrying `class="qmd-error"`: an exception, a timeout,
  or the mid-run "kernel died" marker), so a transient failure re-runs next time. The
  check matches the *class*, not a bare substring, so a cell that merely prints the
  text "qmd-error" still caches.
- **Truncated outputs** (a result clipped at the size cap, marked
  `qmd-fast: output truncated`), so a clipped result is never frozen as if complete.
- **`#| cache: false` cells**, which always re-execute by contract.
- **The cached tail the kernel didn't actually run.** Only cells `[shared, run_end)`,
  the cells that genuinely executed this rebuild, are recorded as the kernel's "ran"
  state; the disk-restored tail is left out, because the live kernel never produced
  it and recording it would falsely claim warm state the kernel doesn't hold.

`QMD_FAST_NO_CACHE` disables the cache outright (every lookup misses, nothing is
written), and "Restart kernel" forces a fresh run rather than a replay.

## The warm kernel (`kernel.rs`)

`Kernel { child, shell, iopub, conn_dir }` is a spawned interpreter plus its ZMQ
client connections. `start()`:

1. picks free ports and writes a Jupyter `connection.json`,
2. spawns the interpreter (`python -m ipykernel` / `R -e IRkernel::main()`) with
   **stderr piped**, and with its **working directory set to the document's own
   directory** (each `Executor` is created `.in_dir(...)` of its page) so a cell's
   relative file writes, audio from `scipy.io.wavfile`, a `#| fig-export:` /
   `ggsave` figure, land beside the source rather than in whatever directory the
   server was launched from,
3. connects the `shell` + `iopub` ZMQ channels, and **races the connect against
   the process exiting**, so a missing `ipykernel` fails in ~1s with its real
   stderr ("No module named ipykernel") instead of hanging the 30s connect
   timeout and reporting something opaque,
4. reads one iopub message to confirm the SUB subscription is live (sidestepping
   the ZMQ slow-joiner problem before the first run), and
5. runs each language's **startup preambles** once against the now-warm kernel: Python
   installs the `ojs_define` Python-to-JS bridge and a matplotlib theme hook that
   restyles inline figures to follow the page (lazily, the first time a cell uses
   matplotlib); R has none.

`execute(code)` sends an `execute_request` on the shell channel and collects iopub
messages parented by that request, namely `stream` (stdout/stderr), `execute_result`,
`display_data`, and `error`, until the kernel returns to `idle`.

A **total wall-clock cap** (`QMD_FAST_CELL_TIMEOUT`, default 120s) guards a runaway
cell. Crucially it is a cap on the whole cell, **not** on the gap between messages,
which is what lets it catch a *streaming* runaway (a `while True: print(...)` that
keeps the channel busy would defeat any per-message idle timeout). On hit, `execute`
SIGINTs the kernel (the `interrupt_mode: signal` path, which surfaces as a
`KeyboardInterrupt` inside the cell) and then drains a short **grace window** (5s) so
the resulting interrupt error and the trailing `idle` arrive and the channels resync,
leaving the warm kernel usable for the *next* cell. If the kernel ignores SIGINT
within the grace window, `execute` gives up on that message and returns what it has.
The same interrupt-then-grace path also fires when the output caps trip
(512 KB of stream text or 4096 output items), so a megabyte-spewing cell stops
flooding the reader rather than being read and discarded. Setting the cap to `0`
disables the wall-clock limit, but a per-output silent-hang backstop (60s with no new
output) still ends a wait that would otherwise hang forever. `Drop` kills the child
and removes the connection dir.

## From a kernel message to HTML

Each collected iopub message is normalised into one `Output` value, and
`render_outputs` turns the list into the HTML that becomes the cell's output block
(@fig-msg-to-html):

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-msg-to-html
%%| fig-cap: "Each iopub message kind maps to one Output, then to a self-contained HTML fragment."
flowchart LR
  stream["stream<br/>(stdout / stderr)"] --> pre["&lt;pre class=qmd-stream&gt;<br/>(+ qmd-stderr)"]
  result["execute_result /<br/>display_data"] --> rich["richest MIME wins:<br/>html › png › svg › jpeg › plain"]
  error["error"] --> err["&lt;pre class=qmd-error&gt;<br/>(ANSI-stripped traceback)"]
```

The mapping is small and explicit:

- **`stream`** becomes a `<pre class="qmd-stream">` (with `qmd-stderr` added for the
  stderr channel), HTML-escaped.
- **`execute_result`** and **`display_data`** are both "rich" outputs; rendering picks
  the **richest representation the kernel offered**, preferring `text/html`, then
  `image/png` (wrapped as an inline `data:` `<img>`), then SVG, then JPEG, then
  `text/plain` (as a `<pre>`). The cell's `text/plain` fallback is only used when
  nothing richer exists.
- **`error`** becomes a `<pre class="qmd-error">` holding the traceback with its ANSI
  colour codes stripped (IPython colourises tracebacks for a terminal). This is the
  one class the freeze cache refuses to store, so an error never sticks.

### Why matplotlib figures render twice

A plain inline matplotlib PNG would bake one foreground colour into the image, so it
would look wrong against the other theme. The Python startup preamble installs (lazily,
the first time a cell touches matplotlib) a `text/html` figure formatter that renders
each figure **twice**, once recoloured for the light theme and once for the dark, and
emits them together as `<img class="qmd-fig qmd-fig-light">` + `<img class="qmd-fig
qmd-fig-dark">`. The standalone `image/png` representation is suppressed so only the
dual-theme HTML survives. The page then swaps which image shows on a `data-theme`
change, so a plot's axes and text always match the surrounding page with no
re-execution, the same trick the theme-matched `{{< video >}}` uses. Only data colours
are left untouched; a `#| fig-export:` writes the *pristine* figure to disk before any
recolouring.

## How generated outputs reach the build

Inline kernel images, a matplotlib figure, an `image/png`, an SVG, are emitted as `data:`
URIs baked straight into the cell's output HTML, so they ship inside the page and need no
sidecar copy at all. A file a cell **writes to disk** (a `#| fig-export:` PNG, a `ggsave`,
audio from `scipy.io.wavfile`) is different: it lands in the document's own directory,
because each `Executor` runs `.in_dir(<doc dir>)` and the kernel inherits that working
directory (see [the warm kernel](#the-warm-kernel-kernel-rs)). The cell then references it
with a relative `src=`, e.g. `<img src="figures/plot.png">`.

The `build` subcommand collects those references so the output is portable, but the two
build shapes do it differently:

- **A single-document `build`** (`build doc.qmd --out <dir>`, or `build doc.qmd out.html`
  into another directory) runs `copy_local_assets` over the rendered HTML **after**
  execution: it scans every `src=`/`href=` value (`local_refs`), keeps the local ones
  (`is_local_ref` drops external URLs, `data:` URIs, in-page anchors), strips any
  `?query`/`#fragment`, and copies each existing file to the same relative path beside the
  page. Because the scan runs after the cells ran, a freshly written `#| fig-export:`
  figure is on disk and gets picked up like any hand-placed image. A separate pass
  (`copy_js_imports`) follows a `{js}` cell's relative `import()`/`fetch()` specifiers,
  which the `src=`/`href=` scan can't see, and `copy_resources` copies a format
  extension's `format-resources` by file name. An **in-place** build (output beside the
  source) skips every self-copy.
- **A site `build`** does not scan HTML at all. `mirror_assets` walks the whole source
  tree once and mirrors every non-source file into `_site/` at the same relative path,
  skipping `.qmd`/`.bib`/`.Rproj` sources, `_`-prefixed and dot entries, and build-cache
  residue (`*_cache`/`*_files`). Since this mirror runs **before** the pages render, a
  figure a cell generates *this* build is not in the mirror unless it was already on disk
  (for instance restored from `_freeze/` on a prior run); a clean rebuild of a doc that
  writes a new sidecar file is the one case to keep in mind.

## Resilience

`ensure_kernel` makes a missing or crashed kernel a recoverable, visible
condition rather than a latch:

- **Crashes mid-run** → the cells *after* the crash **fail fast** with a "kernel
  died" notice instead of each waiting out the full cell timeout on a kernel that
  will never reply; the next rebuild detects the dead kernel, respawns it, and
  re-runs from the top.
- **Failed to start** → back off for `KERNEL_RETRY_AFTER` (20s) before retrying,
  so a bad `QMD_FAST_PYTHON` doesn't re-hang every save, but *fixing* it
  self-heals within a few saves.
- The interpreter's own start error (`last_error`) is surfaced as a diagnostic, so
  "kernel unavailable" tells you *why*.

With no kernel at all, cells render as highlighted source and the preview shows a
quiet "kernel unavailable" note: the document still builds.
